claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain and toughness in structural materials for fusion plasma-facing components are governed by a stress-induced microstructural transition.
The relevant initial state is a disordered high-entropy or refractory alloy exhibiting atomic clustering but no long-range ordering.
Elevated-temperature compressive loading activates thermo-plastic instability.
Thermo-plastic instability produces localized shear bands in which atomistic rearrangements occur.
High-strain compression drives a clustering-to-ordering transition characterized by increased unlike atomic pair correlations and decreased like pair correlations.
Tensile loading does not trigger the same clustering-to-ordering transition and instead maintains a clustered state.
The compression-induced ordering transition is localized within shear bands.
Increased unlike-pair ordering enhances dislocation pinning.
Enhanced dislocation pinning increases strain hardening.
Enhanced strain hardening delays mechanical instability.
Delayed instability increases toughness and plastic strain capacity.
Maintaining the clustered state under tensile loading limits ductility.
High-temperature compression will produce more atomic ordering than tensile loading.
High-temperature compression will produce greater toughness and plastic strain capacity than tensile or low-temperature controls.
At lower temperatures the microstructure remains clustered and consequently exhibits lower strain hardening and toughness.
A controlled comparison should use identical specimens loaded in compression versus tension at 700–1000 K while holding other processing parameters and atmosphere constant.
The mechanism is expected to apply to single-phase high-entropy or refractory alloys with similar atomic diffusivities at 700–1000 K and strain rates sufficient to trigger thermo-plastic instability.
The mechanism may fail in multiphase materials or when irradiation damage or another degradation mechanism dominates.
The proposed 700–1000 K, high-strain-rate, inert-atmosphere tests mimic fusion plasma-facing operating conditions.
Failure to observe either a significant ordering increase or a significant mechanical-property increase under compression relative to tensile controls would falsify the hypothesis.
